Asia’s Market Meltdown Traps Some Traders
 
Plus, restraining Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and one factory’s air-vent demand mystery
 
 
MICHAEL NAGLE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Wall Street has been raking in outsize profits from this year’s market volatility and flashy stock-market debuts, and year-end bonuses are expected to show it.

 

Compensation across Wall Street is expected to rise nearly 4% this year, according to a report from Options Group, an executive search and consulting firm that specializes in financial services. The report is based on data that the firm gathers from clients and candidates, from the start of the year through early November.

 

“Volatility was the defining feature of the past year, and for many firms it proved profitable,” said Michael Karp, chief executive of Options Group.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

A New Generation of Traders Is Trapped in Asia’s Market Meltdown

 

From high-school clubs to social-media influencers, Asia’s new stock traders face a brutal reality check.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Americans and Chinese people are drinking less, and that’s bad news for global consumption, research firm IWSR says. Total consumption of alcoholic drinks dropped 1% on year across 21 key markets over the first six months of this year, according to IWSR data. But stripping out drops of 4% in the U.S. and 3% in China, consumption was up 1% over the period. That “reveals a growing separation in consumption between the world’s two largest markets and the rest of the world,” the study’s authors note. (joshua.kirby@wsj.com; @joshualeokirby)

 

The stronger-than-expected 0.3% rise in the core CPI number in October was similar to September’s in that it was very broad-based, a note from Capital Economics says. “This should all but confirm a December hike, with the strength of inflationary pressures in the last two months raising the risk that the Fed opts for a larger 50bp move rather than 25bp, as Waller has suggested could be a possibility in a hawkish speech today,” the note says. Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller said that if inflation comes in substantially higher than he expects, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)
